Dear list,

I would just like to share a quick function I learned on how to group your observations.

I have a vector of values called "nmv".

[1]  876  876  984  984  976  976 1004 1004  751  751  931  931 1049 1049  963
[16]  963 1071 1071  951  933  933  842  842  969  969 1096 1096 1098 1098 1077

[46]  868 1179 1179 1114 1114 1070 1070  996  996  997  997 1136 1136 1046 1046
[61] 1015 1015  896  896

What I would like to do is group values from different intervals into one variable. I would like them to be characters (and not numbers). I used cars package and function recode(). Notice the use of " and '. I haven't tested if it makes any difference to use any other "quotation marks".

recode(nmv, "600:760='A'; 761:930='B'; 931:1200='C'")

And this is how the above vector looks like after being recoded.

[1] "B" "B" "C" "C" "C" "C" "C" "C" "A" "A" "C" "C" "C" "C" "C" "C" "C" "C" "C"

[58] "C" "C" "C" "C" "C" "B" "B"

If you have any interesting solutions to your problem, don't hesitate to post them.

Cheers,
Roman

The book you mentioned is not out yet.

The original plan was to call this book: "Shit happens". But obviously, this is an inappropriate title for a scientific textbook. However, it does represent the type of data sets that are analyzed in this book; zero inflated data with random effects, zero inflated data with spatial correlation, zero inflated data with temporal correlation, data sets with large number of collinear explanatory variables, binary data with spatial correlation, data measured in transects, etc., etc. The book only contains case studies (with R code).
...
We still expect to finish the book by the end of 2011.

According to my sources, this is "the bible" of multivariate statistics:
Using multivariate statistics <http://www.amazon.com/Using-Multivariate-Statistics-Barbara-Tabachnick/dp/0205459382/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1266496758&sr=8-1-spell>

messages.subject: compilation of R books
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,*

*We made a compilation of books available on R. Not all are known to us,
but we are looking forward to some additional experience.

lp,

Roman and Maarten

Compilation

*Introduction in R*

Alain F. Zuur, Elena N. Ieno, and Erik Meesters. /A Beginner's Guide to
R/. Use R. Springer, 2009. (Users friendly and a nice overview of the
basics of R.)

Michael J. Crawley. /Statistics: An Introduction using R/. Wiley, 2005
(Users friendly and a nice overview of the basics of R, also covers also
other more advanced topics but lacks some details).

Michael J. Crawley. /The R book/. Wiley, 2005 ( a nice overview what is
possible in R, with beginners and advanced topics. It is a more detailed
overview of the statistical methods.)

R in a Nutshell: A Desktop Quick Reference
(http://www.amazon.com/R-Nutshell-Desktop-Quick-Reference/dp/059680170X/ref=pd_sim_b_13)
(Table of contents of this one looks very nice, it basically covers
exactly what we're presenting at the workshop for beginners)

*Statistical modelling*

Alain Zuur, Elena N. Ieno, Neil Walker, Anatoly A. Saveiliev, and
Graham M. Smith. /Mixed Effects Models and Extensions in Ecology with
R/. Springer, New York, 2009. (Great book when you start with mixed
effects models. It is user friendly and has a theoratical part and part
with case studies)

Benjamin M. Bolker. /Ecological Models and Data in R/. Princeton
University Press, 2008.

*Time series*

Jonathan D. Cryer and Kung-Sik Chan. /Time Series Analysis With
Applications in R/. Springer, New York, 2008. ISBN 978-0-387-75958-6.

*Spatial modelling*

Roger S. Bivand, Edzer J. Pebesma, and Virgilio G�mez-Rubio. /Applied
Spatial Data Analysis with R/. Springer, New York, 2008.

Carlo Gaetan and Xavier Guyon. /Spatial Statistics and Modeling/.
Springer Series in Statistics. Springer, 2010.

*Genetical studies*

Andrea S. Foulkes. /Applied Statistical Genetics with R: For
Population-Based Association Studies/. Use R. Springer, 2009.

*Mathematical modelling*

Kai Velten. /Mathematical Modeling and Simulation: Introduction for
Scientists and Engineers/. Wiley-VCH, 2009.

*Graphics*

/ggplot2/:
http://www.amazon.com/ggplot2-Elegant-Graphics-Data-Analysis/dp/0387981403/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1266522052&sr=8-1
<http://www.amazon.com/ggplot2-Elegant-Graphics-Data-Analysis/dp/0387981403/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1266522052&sr=8-1>

(Great book with an introduction how to prepare a nice graph for
publication. It shows nicely how to prepare the graphs with the package
ggplot2.)

/Lattice: Multivariate Data Visualization with R/:
http://www.amazon.com/Lattice-Multivariate-Data-Visualization-Use/dp/0387759689/ref=sr_1_5?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1266522043&sr=8-5
<http://www.amazon.com/Lattice-Multivariate-Data-Visualization-Use/dp/0387759689/ref=sr_1_5?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1266522043&sr=8-5>

*Other statistical books*

A. Zuur, Elena N. Ieno and Graham M. Smith. Amalyzing Ecological Data.
Springer, 2007. (This has no R codes in it but explains verx nicely the
test you can do with R.

For other books see _http://www.r-project.org/_ in the books section.
Other option is Amazone.com. When you found a R book  the slide down the
page with the "Customers Who Bought This Item Also Bought" slide of
Amazone.com can be fruitful as well.

I have received an offer from Lux Libris, a bookstore that deals with scientific literature. They have offered us 15% discount (already calculated into prices). Shipping time is 10-20 days (depends on the book). I have checked some of the prices and they're pretty comparable to those on Amazon.

I will be ordering the following books. If anyone would like to order anything as well, I am willing to lend a hand in handling. Payment is in advance.

Zuur: Mixed effect models and extensions in Ecology with R
Braun: First course in statistical programming with R
Chambers: Software for data analysis: Programming with R

Cheers,
Roman

messages.subject: >odfWeave=R(Sweave)+OpenOffice
messages.body_plain:
Dear Rcoholics,

there are many traps for the aspiring scientist on his/her way to the
land of the reproducible research. There are some tools to help on the
way, too, notably the Sweave package that combines R and latex. There
is a lot of information on that on the internet, among which the
introduction by professor Blejec is very helpful (see his R web page
http://ablejec.nib.si/R/#Sweave).

However, latex code might be intimidating to some and put them off the
noble quest of documenting their code and results in a reproducible
way. The R package odfWeave (http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/
odfWeave/index.html) offers an alternative and couples the R code with
the open office document format. That means that you can use a
powerful text editor Writer, implemented in the free OpenOffice.org
suit, to format your text as well as the output from R (both console
and figure outputs) with the classical Sweave commands. Moreover, you
can format and modify the the final document (such as resize figures,
add captions, modify text etc.) after the  R output has already been
embedded into the text.

I think this implementation of Sweave is really helpful for those who
do not feel quite at home with (la)tex (like myself) and a nice tool
to help us stay on the way of reproducible research. Feel free to give
it a try:

>install.packages(“odfWeave”)
